blocks.text: Carbohydrate metabolism connects immediate ATP production, glucose storage, glucose synthesis, and cellular reducing power. Track three things through each pathway: where the carbon goes, which energy carriers change, and which tissue is doing the work.

blocks.title: Structure changes biological meaning
rows: One sugar unit; different chemistry and enzyme recognition
α versus β forms of a cyclic sugar
Branched glucose reserve in animal tissues

items: Trace glucose through competing metabolic routes
Account for ATP, NADH, and NADPH separately
Explain fed–fasting regulation and tissue differences
Connect enzyme defects to mechanistic consequences

blocks.title: Absorption is not intracellular metabolism
blocks.text: Brush-border digestion yields absorbable monosaccharides. Intestinal glucose and galactose use SGLT1; fructose uses GLUT5. These transport steps precede the intracellular pathways shown below.

Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol. One glucose yields two pyruvate molecules. Two ATP are invested and four are produced: the net is two ATP and two NADH per glucose. These are glycolytic yields, not the total yield from complete glucose oxidation.

blocks.title: Glycolysis: the carbon and ATP checkpoints
blocks.description: A grouped map, not all ten individual reactions. Select checkpoints to inspect their role. [B1, B2]

nodes.title: Glucose
nodes.description: Six-carbon starting substrate.

nodes.title: Glucose-6-phosphate
nodes.description: Hexokinase or glucokinase uses ATP to phosphorylate glucose.

nodes.title: Fructose-6-phosphate
nodes.description: Phosphoglucose isomerase rearranges the six-carbon sugar.

nodes.title: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
nodes.description: PFK-1 consumes the second ATP; this is a major control point.

nodes.title: Two triose streams
nodes.description: Aldolase yields GAP and DHAP. Triose phosphate isomerase converts DHAP to GAP.

nodes.title: Two pyruvate
nodes.description: The payoff reactions form four ATP and two NADH per glucose. Several intermediates are grouped here.

blocks.label: Energy accounting
blocks.text: Gross ATP production is four; net production is two after the investment steps. Conversion of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD⁺ and adds no extra ATP.

blocks.title: A regulator can be both substrate and signal
blocks.text: ATP supplies phosphate to reactions but also signals energy abundance. ATP and citrate inhibit PFK-1; AMP signals low energy availability. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate strongly favors glycolysis.

blocks.prompt: Four ATP are produced and two are invested. What is the net glycolytic ATP yield per glucose?
blocks.answer: Net ATP = 4 − 2 = 2. Keep this separate from NADH and mitochondrial ATP production.

blocks.title: Pyruvate routes: redox, oxidation, and glucose synthesis
blocks.description: Branches represent alternative fates, not a single mandatory sequence. [B2, B5, B12]

nodes.title: Pyruvate
nodes.description: A three-carbon junction between several pathways.

nodes.title: Lactate
nodes.description: Lactate dehydrogenase interconverts lactate and pyruvate while coupling NADH/NAD⁺.

nodes.title: Acetyl-CoA
nodes.description: Pyruvate dehydrogenase forms acetyl-CoA, CO₂, and NADH.

nodes.title: Citric acid cycle
nodes.description: Acetyl units enter an oxidative cycle that produces reduced carriers. This node groups the cycle.

nodes.title: Oxaloacetate
nodes.description: Pyruvate carboxylase uses ATP and biotin to add carbon from bicarbonate.

nodes.title: Glucose synthesis
nodes.description: Oxaloacetate feeds gluconeogenesis through PEP and subsequent bypass reactions.

blocks.label: Direction matters
blocks.text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is not reversed to make glucose. In humans, acetyl-CoA from even-chain fatty acids does not provide net glucose synthesis.

blocks.title: Glycogen synthesis and mobilization
blocks.description: Storage and breakdown use different enzymes; they are not one reversible reaction. [B3, B4]

nodes.title: Glucose-6-phosphate
nodes.description: A shared entry point linking storage and glycolysis.

nodes.title: Glucose-1-phosphate
nodes.description: Phosphoglucomutase interconverts G6P and G1P.

nodes.title: UDP-glucose
nodes.description: An activated glucose donor for glycogen synthesis.

nodes.title: Glycogen
nodes.description: Glycogen synthase extends α1→4 chains; branching enzyme forms α1→6 branches.

nodes.title: Mobilized G1P
nodes.description: Phosphorylase releases G1P from α1→4 links. Debranching handles branch points; a small fraction is free glucose.

nodes.title: Glucose-6-phosphate
nodes.description: G1P is converted to G6P for tissue-specific use.

blocks.prompt: Why can liver glycogen support circulating glucose while skeletal muscle glycogen mainly supports local work?
blocks.answer: Skeletal muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. It cannot directly convert its G6P pool into free glucose for export.

blocks.text: Liver, with a contribution from kidney, makes glucose from precursors such as lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids. Irreversible glycolytic reactions require distinct bypass enzymes. Synthesis of one glucose from two pyruvate costs four ATP, two GTP, and two NADH.

blocks.title: The bypass logic
rows: Pyruvate → OAA → PEP; ATP and GTP required
Produces free glucose in suitable tissues

blocks.title: Fed and fasting states
blocks.text: In the liver, insulin generally favors glucose use and storage. Glucagon favors glucose production and glycogen mobilization. Hormonal regulation changes enzyme activity and expression; it does not override mass balance or tissue-specific enzyme availability.

blocks.prompt: Which pairing bypasses pyruvate kinase during gluconeogenesis?
blocks.answer: Pyruvate first becomes oxaloacetate, then PEP. The bypass consumes energy instead of reversing the pyruvate kinase reaction.

blocks.title: Pentose phosphate pathway: a different currency
PPP: reducing power and pentose carbon
blocks.description: The PPP does not directly make ATP. NADPH serves different functions from NADH. [B6, B7]

nodes.title: Glucose-6-phosphate
nodes.description: Substrate shared with glycolysis and glycogen metabolism.

nodes.title: Oxidative phase
nodes.description: G6PD initiates an irreversible oxidation sequence.

nodes.title: Ribulose-5-phosphate
nodes.description: Oxidation yields a pentose, two NADPH, and CO₂ per G6P.

nodes.title: Ribose-5-phosphate
nodes.description: Pentose interconversion supplies ribose for nucleotide synthesis.

nodes.title: Nonoxidative exchange
nodes.description: Reversible carbon rearrangements adapt pentose supply to demand. Transketolase requires thiamine pyrophosphate.

nodes.title: Glycolytic intermediates
nodes.description: F6P and GAP reconnect pentose metabolism with glycolysis.

blocks.label: Red-cell vulnerability
blocks.text: NADPH supports regeneration of reduced glutathione. G6PD deficiency can impair oxidative defense and cause episodic hemolysis under oxidative stress.

blocks.prompt: Which output is most directly associated with the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway?
blocks.answer: The oxidative phase supplies NADPH. Pentose carbon is also generated; the nonoxidative reactions redistribute it.

blocks.title: Entry routes and defects
rows: Aldolase B deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance
Defects may cause hepatic or muscle-predominant disease

blocks.title: Do not confuse two fructose disorders
blocks.text: Essential fructosuria reflects fructokinase deficiency and is usually benign. Hereditary fructose intolerance reflects aldolase B deficiency and is a clinically serious metabolic disorder.

blocks.title: Ready to explain the system?
items: I can calculate gross versus net glycolytic ATP
I can separate NADH from NADPH functions
I can name the three glycolytic bypasses
I can explain liver–muscle glycogen differences
I can trace the PPP without calling it an ATP-producing pathway

blocks.title: Reading the diagrams
blocks.text: These are deliberately grouped teaching maps. Omitted intermediates, cofactors, and tissue-specific regulation are identified where relevant. Diagrams show mechanistic routes, not quantitative flux simulations.
